title: Anatomy of an AI-driven attack: Bitrise security incident report
content:
Over 25 days an autonomous AI hacking platform probed Bitrise while posing as an authorized penetration test, came back, got in, and was shut out. This is what it did, step by step, and how we stopped it.
An evidence-graded account: how it got in, what it reached, what it did not, how we shut it out, and what every defender should look for.
StatusBitrise is safe to use. The attack path is closed, every production secret and credential we manage was rotated, and we keep watching.
How this report was made
Checked by people. Written with AI help.
AI helped us write this report and build its visuals. The claims, the timeline and the findings were checked by people: our engineers and security engineers. In the age of AI-accelerated attacks, we use AI tools in the response too, so we can report quickly.
Open Evidence under any step to see the log lines behind it.

Times
All times are UTC.
How we countedFirst request from 95.40.73.129 on Oct 25, 01:43 UTC; last request from 118.100.234.120 on Nov 18, 21:19:55 UTC.
How we countedSign-in recorded 11:46:48 UTC; first cloud API call from the attacker’s address with a service-account key 11:57:25 UTC (Nov 13). The key is linked to the secrets revealed minutes earlier by timing: secret values are not logged.
How we countedSuspicious activity detected and investigation initiated 16:32 UTC; shutdown started 19:26 UTC (Nov 13), 7 h 39 min after the sign-in. The platform was switched off at 20:34 UTC.
How we countedFrom the sign-in at 11:46:48 UTC to the last successful cloud API call recorded from the attacker’s addresses at 21:57:50 UTC (Nov 13).
How we countedGoogle Cloud audit logs swept across every project for the attacker’s source addresses: 8,725 entries, 5,662 successful; 72 identities tried, 18 with at least one successful call. A separate search for Nov 18 found 19 more requests, all denied.
How we counted55 minutes, 19 cloud requests all denied, 9 sign-in attempts all refused. One new sign-up was created, never confirmed, and banned.
Summary
Between October 25 and November 18, 2026, an operator pointed ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration-testing platform, at Bitrise. Its agents spent three days in October mapping our public surface under user agents that claimed to be an “authorized pentest”. On November 12 they came back as an ordinary customer, ran their own builds and tested whether one customer could reach another’s files. They could not.
The decisive step came on November 13 at 11:46:48 UTC: a sign-in to a dormant internal test bot account that had no two-factor authentication and still belonged to an internal workspace. Less than eleven minutes later the agents were using cloud keys that belong to that workspace’s projects, and over the next ten hours they chained one credential into the next: Bitrise’s own signing files, source code, infrastructure state and build logs.
We detected suspicious activity at 16:32 UTC, started a platform-wide shutdown at 19:26 UTC and switched the platform off at 20:34 UTC. The last successful cloud call with a stolen key was recorded at 21:57:50 UTC. We then revoked all 919 of our cloud service-account keys, rotated every production secret and credential we manage, and rebuilt our build infrastructure from trusted sources: thousands of servers in three data centers.
When the attacker returned on November 18 and replayed the attack with what it had stolen, every attempt to read anything was refused. We watched it live.
If you are a Bitrise customer
Bitrise is safe to use. The path used in this attack no longer exists.
Most of what the attacker accessed was Bitrise’s own. Files in 15 customer workspaces were accessed without authorization: 1 code-signing certificate file (the attacker could not access the password needed to open it), 1 provisioning profile and 13 diagnostic build logs from May 2026. All 15 customers were contacted immediately.
For every other workspace, our file-level analysis found no evidence of the customer’s secrets, code-signing files, build artifacts or source code in what the attacker accessed. Our logs show no access, and no attempted access, to the store that holds customer secrets.
As a precaution we still recommend rotating the secrets, tokens and certificates you store in Bitrise and reconnecting GitHub. Protected Secret Masked Review shows the last four characters of each secret to help you find them.
This is what an ARTEX-class attack looks like from the receiving end, with exact times, user agents, account names and addresses.
Three fingerprints identify the tool: the client string norma/0.4, things named i<number> (i871-probe, i3694canary), and traffic that announces an “authorized pentest” nobody ordered.
The door was a forgotten account. The damage came from long-lived keys sitting in CI secrets and infrastructure state. The irony of a CI company being breached through a CI bot. We learned.
The techniques were familiar: a forgotten account, secrets that could be revealed, long-lived keys. What stood out was the speed: stolen keys were in use within minutes of being found, and the automation kept probing through the night.
Due to the speed of the spread, Arpad Kun, our VP of Engineering and Infrastructure, made the call: shut the platform down, rotate every production secret and credential we manage rather than only those known to be affected, and rebuild from trusted sources.
In the era of AI-accelerated attacks we need AI-accelerated defense. We now run AI agents that watch activity in real time and investigate what they see. The time of the Defense Agents has arrived.

PrologueOct 25 – Nov 4
It introduced itself as a pentester
For three days an automated client on a cloud address in Hong Kong mapped Bitrise's public surface: 36,698 requests to more than 20 hostnames, five throw-away accounts, and one service it could trick into fetching URLs for it. Its traffic announced an “authorized pentest” that nobody had ordered. It also downloaded a build that one of our customers publishes for its own penetration testing, which tied the scan to activity that looked legitimate. At the time it looked like the scanning every public platform sees every day. Two bursts of sign-ups from Germany and China followed; their link to the attacker is weaker, and we say so.
The lessonTraffic that calls itself an authorized test, when you ordered none, is an attacker introducing itself.
It scans 20+ hostnames and labels its traffic authorized testing
From 95.40.73.129, an AWS address in Hong Kong, the attacker sent 36,698 requests across 20+ Bitrise hostnames. This address was used for discovery and tests. It used ffuf, a tool that tries many URL paths, and user agents including pentest-probe-i5938/1.0 and Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; authorized-pentest/bitrise-readonly).
The tool behind this traffic tells each of its AI agents that it is part of an authorized penetration test, which explains these labels, and is identified in the section “The tool” further down.

report.summary: Bitrise details how an autonomous AI penetration-testing platform breached its CI/CD service via a forgotten bot account, forcing a full shutdown and credential rotation.
report.background: CI/CD platforms like Bitrise sit at the center of the software supply chain: they hold source code, code-signing certificates, provisioning profiles, deploy keys and cloud credentials for thousands of customers. Historically, an intrusion of this depth required weeks of skilled manual work. LLM-driven agent frameworks change the economics — they scan, register accounts, probe authorization boundaries and pivot through credentials automatically, around the clock. ARTEX, the open-source AI pentest platform behind this incident, even instructs its agents to present their traffic as an 'authorized pentest', which is why the October reconnaissance blended in with routine internet noise. The incident pairs two industry trends: years of accumulated long-lived machine credentials stored in CI secrets and infrastructure state, and attackers who can find and reuse those keys within minutes of discovery. Bitrise's report is notable for publishing timestamps, user agents and log evidence, effectively a case study in post-compromise forensics under AI-speed attack.
key_points: Reconnaissance looked like a pentest nobody ordered: 36,698 requests across 20+ Bitrise hostnames from a Hong Kong AWS address (Oct 25–27), five throw-away accounts, ffuf path scanning, and user agents literally declaring 'authorized-pentest/bitrise-readonly'. Two later sign-up bursts from Germany and China were weaker-linked and flagged as such.

The door was a forgotten account. On Nov 13 at 11:46 UTC an agent signed into a dormant internal test bot with no two-factor authentication, still attached to an internal workspace. Eleven minutes later it was calling cloud APIs with that workspace's service-account keys.

Over the next ten hours it chained credentials: 8,725 Google Cloud audit entries from attacker addresses, 5,662 successful, 72 identities attempted and 18 working. It reached Bitrise's own signing files, source code, infrastructure state and build logs — but not customer secrets stores.

Containment was drastic: detection at 16:32 UTC, shutdown initiated 19:26, platform off at 20:34, then all 919 cloud service-account keys revoked, every production secret rotated, and build infrastructure rebuilt from trusted sources across three data centers.

Fifteen customer workspaces were accessed without authorization — one code-signing certificate file (whose password the attacker never obtained), one provisioning profile and 13 May-2026 diagnostic logs. When the attacker replayed the attack on Nov 18, all 19 requests and nine sign-ins were refused live.

The tool has clear fingerprints: client string 'norma/0.4', resources named i<number> such as i871-probe and i3694canary, and traffic announcing an authorized test. Bitrise says the real lesson is speed, and that it now runs AI defense agents watching activity in real time.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is the first detailed public anatomy of an agentic attacker operating end to end: autonomous recon, account creation, authorization probing and credential pivoting, with human-competitive judgment at machine speed. It validates both the offensive promise of AI pentest frameworks and the risk of releasing them openly. For developers and platform teams, the lessons are concrete: kill dormant service accounts, enforce MFA everywhere including internal bots, replace long-lived cloud keys with short-lived federated credentials, and treat CI secrets and Terraform state as crown jewels. For regular users, the blast radius stayed small because no customer secret store was touched, but the incident shows supply-chain breaches increasingly arrive as automated agents rather than human crews — and that vendors may have to take entire platforms offline to stop them. Defensive AI monitoring is shifting from novelty to baseline.
report.tools: Follow ARTEX, the open-source AI pentest framework named here, to understand attacker agent behavior; pair it with ffuf for path fuzzing awareness. On defense, watch agentic monitoring/SIEM tools that baseline service-account behavior, plus secret scanners like Gitleaks and TruffleHog for CI hygiene. Prioritize short-lived credentials through OIDC workload identity federation, hardware-key MFA for all internal accounts, and KMS/HSM-backed signing so certificate files are useless without separate secrets. Bitrise's own report is worth reading as a detection playbook.
